SPLIT (fleet-trunk): items (7) weakening flag + ack and (8) read-only sources moved to B-rc-lifecycle-guard; this task keeps (1)-(6) and the RecordKind.weakening hook used by merge. Declined verbs now carry a reason (RecordKind.declined).

Contract rows RC1, RC2, RC3, RC9 (D-record-surface-contract). Operator 2026-10-11: "so the user or the agent can review, edit, delete, modify, split, evidence is logged".

WHAT: the record lifecycle, built once on the record surface, so goals, principles, rules, decisions, proposals and every later kind get it from their descriptor instead of writing it. Today api/records.py VERBS is list, show, add, edit, remove, search, revise. api/defs.py already has def_supersede and def_merge (and core/defs.py the def.superseded and def.merged events and the merged_from fold) but no surface offers them, `show` cuts the history to the newest 20 entries and keeps only digests (no before/after), a restore is only an unadvertised side effect of `revise`, and split exists for tasks only.
Add these to VERBS, generated on the CLI and as ACTIONS of the kind's one MCP tool (never a new tool; tools/list budget):
(1) `<kind> history <id> [--diff] [--limit N]`: the whole chain read from the log (not the fold's last 20): event, at, by, session, reason, digest; with --diff the field-level before and after (the def.* events carry `fields`; replay by lamport). Redacted, text fenced as data.
(2) `<kind> supersede <id> --by <id2> --reason` (wraps def_supersede; both stay, each names the other).
(3) `<kind> merge <id> [<id>...] --into <id2> --reason`: ONE log transaction: update the target (list fields tags, globs, links, categories are unioned; a scalar is kept unless --take <field>=<id> says otherwise; the text is the caller's: --text or the target's), then def.merged for each source; provenance both ways (the fold already keeps merged_from); refused when kinds differ, a source is not active, or the merge would drop a block-enforcement record into a weaker one without --allow-weaken.
(4) `<kind> split <id> --part <newid>:<field>=<value>[,..] (repeat) --reason` or `--from-file parts.toml`: ONE transaction: each part is a def.recorded with provenance.split_from = <id> (add-time duplicate check among the parts and against the rest, skipping the original), then def.retired of the original with reason and split_into = [ids]. Refuses a single part. No new event kind: split_into / split_from / restored_from are additive optional envelope fields the fold keeps in the history entry (D-compat: an older ddflow preserves what it does not read).
(5) `<kind> restore <id> [--to N|--to <lamport>] --reason`: re-records the fields of the chosen earlier version (default: the last active one) of a retired, superseded, merged or split record as def.recorded with provenance.restored_from; for a merged record the fold already drops it from the absorber's merged_from; for a split it restores the original and says the parts stay.
(6) EVIDENCE stamped on every def write (RC3): api/defs._envelope adds provenance.session (the agent's open session) and provenance.prompt (id of that session's latest session.prompt when there is one) beside `by`; additive. `show` prints them.
(7) WEAKENING FLAG (RC2, D-decision-management 2): RecordKind gains an optional `weakening(before, after) -> reason|""` hook (lower enforcement, widened override, status to retired/dropped/superseded, a guard removed). When the writer is an agent and the hook answers, the event carries weakening=<reason>; the fold exposes unacked agent changes; `<kind> ack <id>` is an OPERATOR-ONLY verb (declared field `operator_only` on RecordKind, honoured by surfaces/exemptions.py: refused on MCP with an explained exit 3) writing ONE new event kind def.acked {kind, id, digest, by}, registered with its first writer and an upcaster stamp. B-dec-manage's `decision ack` is an instance of this verb, not a second mechanism.
(8) READ-ONLY SOURCES (RC9): `readonly(record) -> reason|""` hook; every mutating verb refuses (exit 3) a record whose provenance source is an org bundle, naming source and revision and the local-override path. B-org-kinds registers the provider; with none registered nothing changes.
A kind may opt out of a verb in its descriptor WITH a reason (a proposal is never removed: reject and expire are its tombstones); the conformance test (B-rc-conformance) reads those reasons.

WHY (verified 2026-10-11): without this, five tasks each plan their own edit/retire/supersede/merge path (B199, B-rw-revision, B-coh-resolve, B-dec-manage, B-goal-model) and no task plans split or restore or a history view anywhere; evidence shown to the user is a digest, so 'who changed this rule and from what' cannot be answered after the fact; an agent can silently retire a block rule or drop a goal.

INTERFACE TO REUSE: api/records.py (RecordKind, _pre, _checked, _as), surfaces/records.py (the generator), api/defs.py (def_update, def_retire, def_supersede, def_merge, _envelope), core/defs.py and core/handlers/defs.py (DefRecord.history, merged_from), api/_dedupe.py, surfaces/exemptions.py, surfaces/history_verbs.py (render the new events), core/events.py (register def.acked with its first writer), core/upcasters.py.

chunk_findings.detail: `--to` is resolved lamport-first, so a small integer the caller means as a version number is silently reinterpreted as a lamport. Given a record whose three content events have lamports 2, 7, 9 (it was created as the repo's second event, then other records' events intervened, then two edits): `restore <id> --to 2` intends "version 2" (the middle content event), but `by_lamport = [e for e in content if e.lamport == 2]` is non-empty, so `chosen = by_lamport[0]` is the *first* version and the verb returns OK with `restored_from: 2`. The caller gets version 1's fields back, with no error and a success Outcome — the exact "restore returns the chosen version" claim of the task is violated, and because lamports are global counters that frequently coincide with 1..N, this is not a rare corner. The fallback to `content[to - 1]` only ever runs when no content event happens to carry that lamport, i.e. the version-number form is the exception, not the rule. (`to` is also never validated the way `limit` is validated in `record_history`: `1 <= to <= len(content)` raises TypeError for a non-int `to`, whereas `limit` is explicitly checked for int-ness/non-negativity.)

chunk_findings.detail: The `except` clause catches `(OSError, tomllib.TOMLDecodeError)` but not the decoding error `Path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` raises for a non-UTF-8 file. `read_text` on, say, `assets/logo.png` (a binary file *inside* the repository, so the containment check passes) raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, which derives from `ValueError` — not `OSError`, not `TOMLDecodeError` — so it escapes the handler and the verb blows up with an unhandled exception instead of the clean `(…, why)` refusal the function is written to return. chunk_findings.detail: The change expands `VERBS` to add `history`, `supersede`, `merge`, `split` and `restore`, but the only descriptor it touches — the rules kind (`aliases=("rules",)`) — is set to `verbs=_EVERYDAY` and explicitly declines all five new verbs via `declined={v: _UNWIRED for v in VERBS if v not in _EVERYDAY}`, whose reason defers them to another task. The task's own acceptance and test plan are written entirely on this kind: the acceptance requires `rule add` → `rule edit` → `rule split` → `rule merge` → `rule remove` → `rule restore` to work on CLI and MCP, `rule history <id> --diff` to list each step, and "HOW TO TEST" starts with "merge of two rules". With `split`/`merge`/`restore`/`history` absent from `verbs`, the CLI generator has no subcommand for them and the MCP tool has no such action, so `rule split`, `rule merge`, `rule restore` and `rule history` cannot be invoked at all on the flagship kind — the described acceptance and the (1)–(6) deliverables fail for rules. If the intent really is to wire rules in a later task, this descriptor contradicts the stated scope and acceptance rather than merely deferring it; either the descriptor must offer the verbs (like the other record-surface kinds that get the default `verbs=VERBS`) or the acceptance/test plan must be corrected.

chunk_findings.detail: `append_many` delivers "all of them, or none" only for failures that are raised *inside the Python call stack* of this call, because the rollback lives entirely in the `except BaseException:` block (`os.truncate(self.shard, before)` + `self._lamport = clock`). Each `self.append(...)` inside the loop is written (and, as the docstring's own "truncates this shard back" wording implies, flushed/durable) before the next one runs, and the held `self.transaction()` lock only excludes other writers — it does not protect against the process itself disappearing. Concrete input: a merge calls `append_many([("def.updated", target, ...), ("def.merged", source, ...)])`; after the first `append` returns, the process is killed (SIGKILL / `os._exit` / OOM-killer / power loss after the write reached the page cache or disk). The `except` block never runs, so no truncation and no Lamport restore happen. On the next replay the target's unioned fields and the update are applied while the source is still `active` and names no successor, i.e. the fold contains a permanently half-applied merge (half a split is the same: a `def.recorded` part with no `def.retired`/`split_into` on the original). This is exactly the state the function promises cannot be observed ("a reader never sees half of a merge or a split") and that the "ONE log transaction … a failure injected after the first write leaves nothing half-done" requirement is meant to exclude; the guarantee is exception-scoped, not transaction-scoped, so any non-`except`-mediated termination of the writer leaves the shard inconsistent forever (only a manual repair pass could fix it). Later appends do not re-detect the inconsistency, since nothing records that a multi-event transaction was in flight (no intent marker / WAL entry / txn id in the events themselves).

chunk_findings.detail: The intent fixes the surface signatures as `supersede <id> --by <id2> --reason`, `merge ... --text ...`, and `restore <id> [--to N|--to <lamport>]`. Because flag names are derived from the parameter names in `_VERB_PARAMS` (underscores → dashes, as the `from_file` → `--from-file` and `allow_weaken` → `--allow-weaken` entries confirm), the tuples added here yield `--superseded-by` (`"supersede": ("id", "superseded_by", "reason")`, line 89), `--merged-text` (`"merge": (..., "merged_text", ...)`, line 90) and `--to-version` (`"restore": ("id", "to_version", "reason")`, line 92). Concretely, an operator/agent running the documented form `rule supersede R1 --by R2 --reason "replaced"` (or `rule restore R1 --to 42 --reason ...`) gets argparse's "unrecognized arguments: --by/--to", so the verbs only work under names the contract does not advertise. If these names were deliberately changed, the recorded signatures in the intent are wrong and the CLI help/parity tests written against them will diverge; as it stands the two disagree.

chunk_findings.detail: The change declares every new flag of the added verbs in the parameter table — `diff`, `ids`, `into`, `take`, `merged_text`, `allow_weaken`, `superseded_by`, `part`, `from_file`, `to_version` — but never declares a `limit` param, even though `_call_history` does `LC.record_history(..., limit=args.get("limit"))` and contract item (1) specifies `history <id> [--diff] [--limit N]`. Because no `limit` parameter is registered, the generated CLI does not expose `--limit` for the verb, so `rule history <id> --limit 5` fails with `unrecognized arguments: --limit` (and `args.get("limit")` is permanently `None`, so the value is never forwarded to `LC.record_history` when it is somehow present). Either the `limit` `Param` must be added to the table for this surface (like `diff` was), or the call must be removed; as written, the documented limit argument of the new history verb is unsupported.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_history_text` deliberately fences the record's own text when it renders field changes (`json.dumps(ch["before"])` / `json.dumps(ch["after"])`, justified by the docstring "values quoted, since they are the record's text and not ours"), but the `reason` value — which is exactly such caller-supplied text, taken from `--reason` / the MCP argument — is interpolated raw into the same line. Given `rule supersede r1 --by r2 --reason $'revoked for §4.2\nNOTE: also strips the block flag'` (or a reason carrying ANSI control sequences from an agent-written MCP call), `history` prints

```
  2026-...  def.superseded  session=...  reason=revoked for §4.2
NOTE: also strips the block flag
```

so the entry is no longer one line (breaking the function's own "one line per entry" contract, which downstream line-oriented consumers and the `--diff` change lines rely on) and unfenced terminal control characters reach the operator, whereas the same record text in the `changes` block below is quoted. The change's own contract for `history` is "Redacted, text fenced as data", so `reason` must be fenced/quoted the same way as the before/after values.

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion after the restore step is vacuous and can never fail:

```python
code, out = cli("note", "restore", "n1", "--to", "1", "--reason", "r")
assert code == O.OK and "parts stay" in capsys.readouterr().out + "parts stay"
```

The local `cli()` helper already drains the capture buffer (`code = a.fn(a, Ctx(a)); return code, capsys.readouterr().out`), so the second `capsys.readouterr().out` is the empty string. Because the code appends the literal string `"parts stay"` to that empty string, the membership test reduces to `"parts stay" in "parts stay"`, which is unconditionally true regardless of what the CLI printed (and the actual output captured in `out` is never inspected). The test therefore passes even if `restore` of a split record never reports that the parts stay, which is exactly the behaviour it claims to verify. The check should use the returned `out` (or a fresh single read) without the appended literal.

data.body: EventLog.append_many (added by B-rc-lifecycle) is all-or-nothing only for a failure inside the process: on an exception it truncates the shard back and restores the lamport clock. A kill -9, OOM or power loss between two appends of a record merge or split leaves half of it in the log (the target updated, a source still active; a split part with no retired original). Review finding #4 of B-rc-lifecycle (rubber_duck). Fix: stamp the events of a batch with a shared batch id and count, and have the fold hold a batch's events back until all arrive (older ddflow ignores the unknown fields and applies each event as today: D-compat additive); doctor reports an incomplete batch and offers a repair. Regression test: kill the writer between the appends and fold.
data.title: A multi-event log write (merge, split) is crash-atomic: a batch marker the fold ignores until complete

chunk_findings.detail: `_envelope` assembles provenance as `{"by": cfg.agent.id, **(provenance or {}), **stamp}`. The caller-supplied `provenance` is spread *after* `by`, and `stamp` (the new `evidence()` result) only overrides `session`/`prompt` and only when a live session exists. The change simultaneously declares `STAMPED = ("by", "session", "prompt")` as "keys the writer stamps itself on every write ... never carried over from an earlier revision", but nothing in the code applies that filter: `STAMPED` is not used in `_envelope`, and no stripping of `provenance` happens before the spread. So any caller that passes a carried-over provenance (precisely the case the `STAMPED` contract is documented for, e.g. re-recording a prior revision's fields) has its old values win. Concretely, `_envelope(cfg, "rule", "r1", None, {"by": "<operator-id>"}, log)` returns `by="<operator-id>"` even though the write is made by an agent. Because the RC2 weakening flag (and the RC3 evidence) key off the writer being an agent, an agent that reconstructs provenance with `by=<operator>` produces a log entry that looks operator-authored, so a lowered enforcement (block→warn) is never recorded as `weakening=` and never appears as awaiting acknowledgement. The same hole lets a stale `session`/`prompt` from the earlier revision survive whenever the current writer has no open session, attributing the edit's evidence to the wrong session/prompt. The fix is to drop the `STAMPED` keys from `provenance` (or place `by` after the spread) before recording.

chunk_findings.detail: The no-op detection compares two sides that are stripped differently. chunk_findings.detail:
`append_many` does not make the batch atomic; it makes it *undoable by byte offset*, and it does that while holding only the append lock.

```python
before = self.shard.stat().st_size if self.shard.exists() else 0
...
for kind, subject, data in items:
    out.append(self.append(kind, subject, data))   # events become visible one by one
except BaseException:
    os.truncate(self.shard, before)                # deletes whatever is after `before`
```

Concrete interleaving: process A runs `rule merge R1 R2`, so `append_many` writes `def.updated R1` (carrying the merge reason) and then `self.append` for the second item raises; the rollback truncates. In the window between the first `append` and the failure, process B running `rule show R1` (a read) folds an R1 whose history contains the merge's provenance update but no `def.merged` for R2 — exactly the "half of a merge or a split" the docstring claims a reader can never see. If the batch then rolls back, B has consumed an event that no longer exists at all, so two reads taken moments apart disagree about whether the merge happened. The docstring's own wording ("The append lock is held throughout") gives the game away: it is the *append* lock, so it excludes writers, not readers, and the "a reader never sees half of a merge" guarantee is unsupported by the code.

The same truncate is also destructive beyond the batch: `os.truncate(self.shard, before)` removes every byte after `before`, regardless of who wrote it. If any write path reaches the shard without going through this same transaction (a second process/CLI/MCP invocation whose append does not share the lock), and it lands in that window, the merge's failure silently deletes a committed, unrelated event. Nothing in `append_many` verifies exclusivity, so its correctness rests on an invariant the function neither establishes nor checks. Making the batch invisible until commit needs a temp segment + rename, or readers and all writers taking the same lock.

chunk_findings.detail: The new history formatter prints the per-entry columns `at`, `event`(+`version`), `by`, and the optional `session`, `reason`, `successor`, `split_into`, `split_from`, `restored_from` — but it never reads `h["digest"]`, so the digest column required by RC1 ("the whole chain … event, at, by, session, reason, digest") is absent from the output. Given a record with a couple of revisions, `rule history <id>` renders only `at / event / by / session / reason`, and an operator cannot quote the entry's digest to reference one specific logged event, which is exactly the evidence handle the entry is supposed to carry. chunk_findings.detail: `_envelope` assembles provenance as `{"by": cfg.agent.id, **(provenance or {}), **stamp}`. The caller-supplied `provenance` is spread *after* `by`, and `stamp` (the new `evidence()` result) only overrides `session`/`prompt` and only when a live session exists. The change simultaneously declares `STAMPED = ("by", "session", "prompt")` as "keys the writer stamps itself on every write ... never carried over from an earlier revision", but nothing in the code applies that filter: `STAMPED` is not used in `_envelope`, and no stripping of `provenance` happens before the spread. So any caller that passes a carried-over provenance (precisely the case the `STAMPED` contract is documented for, e.g. re-recording a prior revision's fields) has its old values win. Concretely, `_envelope(cfg, "rule", "r1", None, {"by": "<operator-id>"}, log)` returns `by="<operator-id>"` even though the write is made by an agent. Because the RC2 weakening flag (and the RC3 evidence) key off the writer being an agent, an agent that reconstructs provenance with `by=<operator>` produces a log entry that looks operator-authored, so a lowered enforcement (block→warn) is never recorded as `weakening=` and never appears as awaiting acknowledgement. The same hole lets a stale `session`/`prompt` from the earlier revision survive whenever the current writer has no open session, attributing the edit's evidence to the wrong session/prompt. The fix is to drop the `STAMPED` keys from `provenance` (or place `by` after the spread) before recording.

chunk_findings.detail: The no-op detection compares two sides that are stripped differently. The right side, `unstamped`, is the recorded provenance *with the writer-stamped keys removed* (`{k: v for k, v in rec.provenance.items() if k not in STAMPED[1:]}`), but the left side, `{"by": cfg.agent.id, **prov}`, is built from the caller's mapping verbatim and is *not* stripped. Because every write now stamps `session`/`prompt` into `provenance` (RC3), any caller that hands back the record's own provenance — the pattern the previous code explicitly treated as a no-op, since it compared `{"by": cfg.agent.id, **prov} == rec.provenance` — is now always judged a provenance change. Concretely, `def_update(repo, kind, rid, {}, provenance={**rec.provenance})` with no field change used to return `O.nothing` ("nothing changed", exit 2); with this code the two sides can never match (the left carries `session`/`prompt`, `unstamped` cannot), so it writes a redundant `def.updated` event and returns `O.ok` (exit 0), directly contradicting the comment on the very next line: "an update that changes nothing else is exit 2 whoever asks". It also inflates `history --diff` with an entry whose `fields` and `digest` are unchanged. Fix: strip `STAMPED`/`STAMPED[1:]` from the supplied mapping too, so both sides are compared on the same keys.

The target side of a merge is invisible to the new `history` verb. `record_merge` writes `def.merged` events whose subject is the *source* (`log.append_many` line `writes.append(("def.merged", D.key(kind.def_kind, src.id), body))`), and the only write against the target is the `def.updated` produced by `DEFS._update_data(...)`; nothing in that update carries the source ids (the target's `merged_from` is only ever materialised by the fold). `record_history` deliberately reads the chain from the log (`_chain` filters `e.subject == key`) and `_entries` surfaces only the fixed key list `event, at, by, lamport, version, session, prompt, reason, digest, successor, split_into, split_from, restored_from` — `merged_from` is not in that list.

chunk_findings.detail:
`append_many` does not make the batch atomic; it makes it *undoable by byte offset*, and it does that while holding only the append lock.

```python
before = self.shard.stat().st_size if self.shard.exists() else 0
...
for kind, subject, data in items:
    out.append(self.append(kind, subject, data))   # events become visible one by one
except BaseException:
    os.truncate(self.shard, before)                # deletes whatever is after `before`
```

Concrete interleaving: process A runs `rule merge R1 R2`, so `append_many` writes `def.updated R1` (carrying the merge reason) and then `self.append` for the second item raises; the rollback truncates. In the window between the first `append` and the failure, process B running `rule show R1` (a read) folds an R1 whose history contains the merge's provenance update but no `def.merged` for R2 — exactly the "half of a merge or a split" the docstring claims a reader can never see. If the batch then rolls back, B has consumed an event that no longer exists at all, so two reads taken moments apart disagree about whether the merge happened. The docstring's own wording ("The append lock is held throughout") gives the game away: it is the *append* lock, so it excludes writers, not readers, and the "a reader never sees half of a merge" guarantee is unsupported by the code.

The same truncate is also destructive beyond the batch: `os.truncate(self.shard, before)` removes every byte after `before`, regardless of who wrote it. If any write path reaches the shard without going through this same transaction (a second process/CLI/MCP invocation whose append does not share the lock), and it lands in that window, the merge's failure silently deletes a committed, unrelated event. Nothing in `append_many` verifies exclusivity, so its correctness rests on an invariant the function neither establishes nor checks. Making the batch invisible until commit needs a temp segment + rename, or readers and all writers taking the same lock.

chunk_findings.detail: `declare()` now registers every kind for which `kind.stored_kind` is true into the derived surface (`PA.declare(... search=kind.search, recall=kind.recall, ...)`). The `RULE` descriptor sets `recall=False, resource=False` and its comment states "rules keep their own search source … (their output is pinned)", but it does **not** set `search=False`, so `rule.search` keeps its default (the intent says "search (default on)"). `rule` is a stored kind (`def_kind` in `D.DEF_KINDS`), so it is registered into the derived `records` source with search enabled at the same time that services/search.py still keeps `rule` among "today's legacy entries" for byte-for-byte golden output. Concretely, with the legacy hand-listed `rule` source and the new derived `records` source both active, `ddflow search --kind rule` (and any untyped search) yields rule hits from both sources — duplicated/changed hits — which violates the change's own requirement that "rule, skill, agent, schedule and decision golden outputs of search and recall are byte-identical" and contradicts the descriptor comment. chunk_findings.detail: `_resource_text(..., full=True)` builds the history digest with `f"... first {rec.at[:10]}, last {rec.updated_at[:10]} ..."` and indexes `rec.updated_at` unconditionally. The sort key two functions below (`key=lambda r: (r.updated_at or r.at, r.id)`) explicitly guards against a falsy `updated_at` by falling back to `at`, which shows the author expects records to exist whose `updated_at` is `None`/empty. For such a record (e.g. one created and never modified, or one persisted before the update-timestamp was introduced), the list resource works — it is produced by `_resource_text(kind, r, False)`, which never touches `updated_at` and uses the `or r.at` key — so the record is advertised in `ddflow://records/<kind>`; but reading that same advertised URI goes through `record_resource_read` → `_resource_text(kind, rec, True)` → `rec.updated_at[:10]`, raising `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`. The read fails (500 / MCP error) for a record the listing just offered, instead of returning it. The same line also means the digest's "last" timestamp disagrees with the ordering key used to sort the list (`updated_at or at` vs `updated_at` alone). Fix by using the same `rec.updated_at or rec.at` fallback (and guarding `rec.at` likewise) for the "last" field.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new guard that hides a declared kind's event rows from the `log` source is:

```
if any(d.searched and d.def_kind == kind and d.name in kinds
       and (not names or "records" in names) for d in PA.DECLARED.values()):
    continue
```

`names` is the source-name set derived from the *requested* kinds via `_OWNER` (that is the only way the pre-existing `if kind in _RECORD_SOURCES and held(kind)` check can work), and `_OWNER` is not extended for declared kinds. So `"records"` lands in `names` only when some requested kind is one of `_RECORD_SOURCES`; when the request contains only a declared kind, `names` is empty and `not names` saves the suppression. The gap is a mixed request: given `ddflow search --kind goal,rule` (or `--kind goal,skill`, `--kind goal,session`), `kinds = {"goal","rule"}`, so `d.name in kinds` is true, but `names == {"defs"}` is non-empty and does not contain `"records"`, so the condition is false. The goal's event is therefore emitted as a normal `log` row (`Doc("log", ev.id, ev.kind, …)`) while `_declared_docs` (`_RecordsSource.hits`, same file) also emits the same goal under the declared kind, with a different id and source. The record is returned twice with its content duplicated, and ranking scores both, whereas `--kind goal` alone or `--kind goal,task` returns it once; suppression of a declared kind's log row must not depend on which other kinds were requested, only on that declared kind being requested and being served by the `records` source.

chunk_findings.detail: `declare()` now registers every kind for which `kind.stored_kind` is true into the derived surface (`PA.declare(... search=kind.search, recall=kind.recall, ...)`). The `RULE` descriptor sets `recall=False, resource=False` and its comment states "rules keep their own search source … (their output is pinned)", but it does **not** set `search=False`, so `rule.search` keeps its default (the intent says "search (default on)"). `rule` is a stored kind (`def_kind` in `D.DEF_KINDS`), so it is registered into the derived `records` source with search enabled at the same time that services/search.py still keeps `rule` among "today's legacy entries" for byte-for-byte golden output. Concretely, with the legacy hand-listed `rule` source and the new derived `records` source both active, `ddflow search --kind rule` (and any untyped search) yields rule hits from both sources — duplicated/changed hits — which violates the change's own requirement that "rule, skill, agent, schedule and decision golden outputs of search and recall are byte-identical" and contradicts the descriptor comment. chunk_findings.detail: `_resource_text(..., full=True)` builds the history digest with `f"... first {rec.at[:10]}, last {rec.updated_at[:10]} ..."` and indexes `rec.updated_at` unconditionally. The sort key two functions below (`key=lambda r: (r.updated_at or r.at, r.id)`) explicitly guards against a falsy `updated_at` by falling back to `at`, which shows the author expects records to exist whose `updated_at` is `None`/empty. For such a record (e.g. one created and never modified, or one persisted before the update-timestamp was introduced), the list resource works — it is produced by `_resource_text(kind, r, False)`, which never touches `updated_at` and uses the `or r.at` key — so the record is advertised in `ddflow://records/<kind>`; but reading that same advertised URI goes through `record_resource_read` → `_resource_text(kind, rec, True)` → `rec.updated_at[:10]`, raising `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`. The read fails (500 / MCP error) for a record the listing just offered, instead of returning it. The same line also means the digest's "last" timestamp disagrees with the ordering key used to sort the list (`updated_at or at` vs `updated_at` alone). Fix by using the same `rec.updated_at or rec.at` fallback (and guarding `rec.at` likewise) for the "last" field.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new guard that hides a declared kind's event rows from the `log` source is:

```
if any(d.searched and d.def_kind == kind and d.name in kinds
       and (not names or "records" in names) for d in PA.DECLARED.values()):
    continue
```

`names` is the source-name set derived from the *requested* kinds via `_OWNER` (that is the only way the pre-existing `if kind in _RECORD_SOURCES and held(kind)` check can work), and `_OWNER` is not extended for declared kinds. So `"records"` lands in `names` only when some requested kind is one of `_RECORD_SOURCES`; when the request contains only a declared kind, `names` is empty and `not names` saves the suppression. The gap is a mixed request: given `ddflow search --kind goal,rule` (or `--kind goal,skill`, `--kind goal,session`), `kinds = {"goal","rule"}`, so `d.name in kinds` is true, but `names == {"defs"}` is non-empty and does not contain `"records"`, so the condition is false. The goal's event is therefore emitted as a normal `log` row (`Doc("log", ev.id, ev.kind, …)`) while `_declared_docs` (`_RecordsSource.hits`, same file) also emits the same goal under the declared kind, with a different id and source. The record is returned twice with its content duplicated, and ranking scores both, whereas `--kind goal` alone or `--kind goal,task` returns it once; suppression of a declared kind's log row must not depend on which other kinds were requested, only on that declared kind being requested and being served by the `records` source.

chunk_findings.detail: The RULE descriptor disables recall and resources but leaves `search` at its default (on), while the comment immediately above it states "rules keep their own search source". `declare()` forwards `search=kind.search` into the newly added `PA.declare(...)` call, and the change's own intent says the derived source "registers every descriptor with a def_kind". Rule's `def_kind` is one of the four legacy kinds that already have a hand-written source in `services/search.py` (the intent says those sources are preserved so "rule, skill, agent, schedule keep their output byte for byte"). With `search` still True, `ddflow search --kind rule <query>` will emit each matching rule twice — once from the legacy rule source and once from the derived `records` source — so the pinned/golden search output is no longer byte-identical and duplicate hits are user-visible. The fix implied by the comment is `search=False` alongside the other two flags (until the legacy rule source is retired).

chunk_findings.detail:
The newest-first sort in `record_resource_read` deliberately guards against a missing `updated_at`:

```python
key=lambda r: (r.updated_at or r.at, r.id),
```

so a record whose `updated_at` is empty/`None` is sorted fine and appears in `resources/read ddflow://records/<kind>`. But the single-record path calls `_resource_text(kind, rec, True)`, which formats the history digest as

```python
f"history: {len(events)} entries, first {rec.at[:10]}, last {rec.updated_at[:10]} ..."
```

without the `or rec.at` fallback used two functions above. For exactly the record the sort code was written to tolerate (`updated_at` falsy, or `at` falsy), `resources/read ddflow://records/<kind>/<id>` raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable` (or `AttributeError`) instead of returning the record. The list resource (`full=False`) never touches those fields, so the same record reads fine as part of the list but 500s/raises on the per-record URI — the inconsistency is internal to this diff and needs no assumption about the data beyond what the sort guard already states.

chunk_findings.detail: `unregister()` mutates `self.table` directly but, unlike `__contains__`, `names()`, `__len__`, `values_list()` and `listing()`, it never calls `self._fill()`. For any registry built with `package=`/`prefix=` (or `loader=`) that has not been accessed yet, the table is still empty, so `pop(name, None)` removes nothing and the call silently no-ops — while the very next access (`get_or_raise`, `in`, `names`) runs `_fill()`, imports the `kind_*.py` module and puts the name straight back. Concrete input: `reg = Registry("export kind", package="ddflow.kinds", prefix="kind_")` (fresh, never read); `reg.unregister("kind_x")`; then `reg.get_or_raise("kind_x")` — instead of the `UnknownName` the docstring promises for a removed name, discovery re-registers it and the item is returned. A test that uses the documented "a test's throwaway" removal to exercise the unknown-name path therefore cannot work on a discovery-backed registry. `register()` has the mirror-image hole (a pre-`_fill` `register(stub, "kind_x")` succeeds, then the later `_fill()` import raises `DuplicateName` from the module being discovered), so the fix is to fill before mutating, or to defer the mutation until the registry is ready.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/registry.py:unregister

chunk_findings.detail: The retry contract ("a failure raises again on the next call (nothing is half-marked as done)") only holds for eager loaders. `_ready = True` is assigned after the loop, so a loader failure leaves `_ready` False and `_fill` re-runs — but items already handed to `register()` are still in `self.table`, and a generator loader re-yields them. Input: `Registry("gate kind", loader=lambda: (d for d in load_toml_files()))`, where `load_toml_files()` yields three valid descriptors and then raises `OSError` on a fourth file. First call registers items 1–3 and propagates `OSError`. Second call re-runs the generator, hits item 1 again, and `register()` (default `same_ok=False`) raises `DuplicateName` instead of the original error; even after the fourth file is fixed, the process can never complete the fill. Package discovery is unaffected only because `importlib.import_module` caches successful modules, so the asymmetry is easy to miss.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/registry.py:_fill

chunk_findings.detail:
`registered()` used to return the ticks in a deterministic, explicitly sorted order:
```python
return [REGISTRY[n] for n in sorted(REGISTRY)]
```
The new body is `return REGISTRY.values_list()`, and — unlike the search-source registry in the same change (`SOURCES = Registry(..., order="registered")`) and unlike the old sorted implementation — the ticks registry is constructed with **no** order argument:

```python
REGISTRY: Registry[Tick] = Registry("tick", key=lambda t: t.name, same_ok=True)
```

so `registered()`'s order is now whatever the helper's default happens to be, rather than the alphabetical order the old code guaranteed. With ticks registered in non-alphabetical order (e.g. `register(Tick(name="zebra"))` then `register(Tick(name="alpha"))`), the old call returned `[alpha, zebra]`; the new call returns them in the registry's default order, which for a registry that defaults to insertion/registration order is `[zebra, alpha]`. That changes the output of every consumer of `ticks.registered()` (doctor/help listings, scheduler iteration) while the change's own regression claim only covers "the same names", so a set-vs-list comparison of names would not catch it. If the intended contract is still sorted-by-name, this construction needs `order="name"` (or the sort must be reinstated); if the intended contract is now registration order, the change from the previous sorted behaviour needs to be called out rather than dropped silently.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ticks.py: registered()

chunk_findings.detail:
`_fill` only sets `_ready = True` after the whole package import *and* the loader run, but it writes into `self.table` as it goes (`self.register(item)` at line 140). On a loader that fails part-way the table is left half-populated while `_ready` stays `False`, so the docstring's promise ("nothing is half-marked as done", line 130) is false in the direction that matters, and the retry is broken. Concrete input:

```python
def loader():
    yield "a"                     # registered into the table
    raise RuntimeError("bad descriptor in kinds.toml")

reg = Registry("export kind", key=str, loader=loader)
reg.names()   # RuntimeError: bad descriptor ... ("a" is now in reg.table, _ready is False)
reg.names()   # DuplicateName: export kind 'a' is already registered
```

The second call never re-raises the real error: `"a"` survived the failed fill, so `register` hits `have is not None` at line 109 and raises `DuplicateName` instead. Worse, this is permanent without `same_ok`/`replace`: even after the underlying TOML problem is fixed, every subsequent `names()`/`get()`/`in` keeps failing on `"a"` rather than completing discovery, so the registry is wedged for the life of the process (only `unregister("a")` or a fresh process recovers). The same masking applies to any consumer call that triggers the fill (`__len__`, `__contains__`, `values_list`, `listing`), so a doctor/help listing reports a bogus "duplicate" error for a registry whose loader only ever failed once. Making the fill atomic (fill a staging dict, or set an in-progress/ready marker visible to reentrant/retried calls) is what the documented behaviour requires.

chunk_findings.detail: `HARNESSES` is a module-level `Registry(..., order="registered", loader=load)`, and the added docstring states it is "loaded on first use", i.e. the registry loads `load()` once and thereafter serves entries out of its own table. Previously `get()` and `ids()` called `load()` on *every* call, and `load()` is a per-root cache (`_cache[root]`), i.e. its result is a function of a root chosen at call time and it is invalidated by clearing `_cache`. With the new module-level registry, the first `load()` result is frozen for the life of the process: a caller that first exercises `get()`/`ids()` for one root and later asks for another root (or a test that monkeypatches the harness root and clears `harnessreg._cache`) will get the descriptors/ids of the *first* root back, because `HARNESSES.get()`/`HARNESSES.names()` no longer re-invoke `load()` and re-registering the new set is exactly what the duplicate-name guard forbids. Concretely: `get("claude")` in process where root has already been resolved once returns the descriptor for that first root even after the root/`_cache` changes, which is a regression from `next((h for h in load() if h.id == agent), None)`.
